title: Documents Between Companies: EDI, Punchout and E-Invoicing
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/22-edi-and-e-invoicing/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (a thesis paragraph p05, a roadmap p06, and a conclusion paragraph p52 that answers the opening); p04 is rewritten to pick up the B2B chapter as this chapter's transition_in asks.

know: The EDI vocabulary: standards (UN/EDIFACT with GS1 EANCOM, ANSI X12), messages (ORDERS, ORDRSP, DESADV or ASN, INVOIC, CONTRL), identifiers (GTIN, GLN, SSCC), transports (AS2, SFTP, VAN, Peppol), per-partner guidelines and mappings, and the two families of chargebacks (delivery performance, data and label compliance).
That a syntax acknowledgment says only that a file could be parsed, and that a punchout cart is not an order.

The layers of an e-invoice (EN 16931, UBL, Peppol BIS Billing 3.0), the difference between an EDI INVOIC and a Peppol invoice, and the mandate calendar as of November 2026 (Belgium since 1 January 2026, Germany issuing from 2027 or 2028, the Netherlands planned for 2030, ViDA's cross-border reporting from 1 July 2030), with the domestic scope of the Belgian and German mandates.
believe: Each document has one honest source: the order record from the buyer's message, the despatch advice from the warehouse's pack confirmation, the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment; a compliance chargeback is a document generated in the wrong place.
An EDI order is a channel into the order record, not a separate order system.
E-invoicing is a legal calendar that makes delivery status part of the invoice, and the company must hold the knowledge of each mapping even when its provider holds the mapping.
can_do: Explain a compliance chargeback by the system that generated the document, and say which system should generate each document.
Place their own company on the mandate calendar, and write a partner card (GLNs, transport, message and guideline versions, mapping version, internal owner, compliance rules, open disputes).
Choose among a provider's portal, an integrated provider, in-house EDI and an e-document gateway by partners and countries.

audience.who: Newcomers to commerce architecture; most of all an integration engineer or product manager who inherits a wholesale channel and is asked why a retail chain deducted money, and a finance or engineering lead who hears 'Peppol' for the first time. Also an architect choosing between a provider's portal, an integrated provider, in-house EDI and an e-document gateway.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.

From earlier chapters: Kestrel & Pine, its people and incidents in outline; the order record, systems of record, single writer, idempotency and reconciliation; the WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI (named), OMS, SKU and GTIN; Waypoint decisions W1–W8 in outline.
From Part III: one invoice per shipment issued by the ERP, credit notes as the only correction, and the Belgian Peppol invoice to Ardennes Trail Co. in outline.
From the B2B chapter: company accounts, contract prices, terms and credit owned by the ERP, the portal, and the buyer's own system (EDI or punchout) named as a fourth channel option.
does_not_know: EDIFACT, EANCOM, X12, ORDERS, ORDRSP, DESADV/ASN, INVOIC, CONTRL/997, GLN, SSCC, AS2, SFTP, VAN, Peppol and its access points, the four-corner model, mapping and message implementation guidelines, supplier chargebacks.
EN 16931, UBL, Peppol BIS Billing 3.0, clearance, ViDA and the national mandate dates.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a deduction for despatch advices that did not match the pallets, the reader names the system that wrote them, why they differed and what should generate each document, not better pickers.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A retail chain deducts money from a supplier's payment because pallet labels did not match the despatch advices it received. The supplier's ERP sends each despatch advice when the order is released to the warehouse; the warehouse system prints pallet labels at packing, and pickers sometimes merge or split pallets. Using only this chapter: why did the labels and the messages differ, and what should generate each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The despatch advice was written from the order before anything was packed, with pallet numbers from an ERP range, so merged or split pallets made it describe different pallets from those on the truck. The SSCC labels and the despatch advice must both come from the warehouse system's pack confirmation, the system that builds the pallet; each DESADV is compared with the pack confirmation before it is sent; and a partner card per trading partner keeps the mapping knowledge inside the company rather than in one consultant's head. Not better pickers or a new EDI provider alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a Dutch brand with business customers in three countries, the reader states which e-invoicing rules reach it and from when, hedging where the sources do, and what its invoicing system must keep.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch brand invoices business customers in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. Using only this chapter: which e-invoicing rules apply to it or to its customers, from when, and what must its invoicing system keep for each invoice?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Belgium has required structured e-invoices over Peppol between Belgian VAT-registered businesses since 1 January 2026; whether that binds a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment is not settled, but the Belgian customers' bookkeeping expects Peppol invoices. Germany's mandate (receive since 2025, issue from 2027, or 2028 for small businesses) covers businesses established in Germany. The Netherlands plans invoicing from 1 July 2030, and ViDA's cross-border reporting starts 1 July 2030. The system that numbers and issues invoices (usually the ERP) stores each invoice's transmission status, rejections and archive, with a daily report of invoices issued but not delivered.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what a repeated ORDERS file and a CONTRL acknowledgment each mean.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: the EDI provider re-sends an ORDERS file after a timeout that was in fact a success, and the supplier receives a CONTRL acknowledgment for an invoice it sent. What does each mean, and how should the supplier treat them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The buyer's order number plus its GLN is the order's natural key, so a second ORDERS with the same key is a duplicate or a change, never a new order (idempotent handling). A CONTRL says only that the file could be parsed, not that the invoice was accepted or will be paid; acceptance and payment come in later messages and in the payment itself.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How companies trade by exchanging standard documents (a purchase order, a shipment notice per pallet, an invoice the buyer's software can read); why each document must come from a different system (the order record, the warehouse's pack confirmation, the ERP's confirmed shipment); which e-invoicing deadlines already apply (Belgium since 1 January 2026 over Peppol, Germany from 2027, the Netherlands planned for 2030) and why the invoice becomes a transmitted document with a delivery status. In order: a deduction Bergzicht made from a payment; what EDI is and why it persists, its documents, identifiers, transport and partner rules; which system each document must come from and where punchout fits; the e-invoice and the calendar of mandates; the ways to connect and how they change with scale; Bergzicht's spring reorder of April 2027 and a Belgian invoice worked through, sharing Duiven's warehouse system and the books with web orders; what goes wrong. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's deduction, the GS1 and X12 standards, retailers' published supplier conditions and official mandate pages.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How do large trading partners exchange orders, shipping notices and invoices without a web shop, and what do e-invoicing mandates require?
thesis.claim: Trading partners exchange orders, despatch advices and invoices as standard EDI messages, mapped per partner and relayed by a provider or a direct link; each document has one internal source: the order enters the order record like a web order, the despatch advice comes from the warehouse's pack confirmation, the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment. E-invoicing mandates require structured invoices from dated, country-specific deadlines, so the ERP that issues them holds each invoice's transmission status.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that EDI is a back-office file exchange the EDI provider or a consultant looks after: the ERP may generate every outgoing document from the order, EDI orders may stay in the ERP or the provider's portal apart from web orders, and e-invoicing is a question of PDF formats to answer when a customer asks.
thesis.so_what: In Q3 2026 Kestrel & Pine's ERP wrote Bergzicht's despatch advices when wholesale orders were released, before packing, with ERP pallet numbers, while the WMS labeled the pallets it actually built; Bergzicht deducted €14,200 for nine deliveries, and only an external consultant knew the mappings. Under W6 the WMS generates the SSCC labels and the despatch advice at pack confirmation and a partner card per trading partner holds the mapping knowledge, so Bergzicht's 240-unit reorder of 6 April 2027 ships on three pallets whose labels and message describe the same pallets. A merchant that accepts the claim routes each document from its one source and keeps a dated mandate calendar with an owner per country before the first chain or foreign business customer asks.
thesis.how_why: A chain's receiving scans each pallet's SSCC label against the despatch advice, so a message written from the order before packing is wrong whenever pickers merge or split pallets; only the system that builds and labels the pallet knows what is on it. The invoice is a payment claim for what was delivered at agreed prices with VAT, so it comes from the system that holds the confirmed shipment, the prices and the legal numbering. An EDI order is a purchase commitment like a web order, so if it lives apart, allocation, invoicing and reporting see two shapes. Each partner's guideline changes on its own schedule and is enforced by chargebacks, so the knowledge of each mapping must sit inside the company. Under a mandate an invoice exists for the receiver only once the network delivers it, and in clearance countries only once the state accepts it, so delivery and rejection become states the issuing system must hold.

supporting_claims.claim: Trading partners exchange a small set of standard documents (order, order response, despatch advice, invoice, acknowledgment) built on shared identifiers, carried point-to-point or over a network, and mapped to each partner's own guideline, which the buyer chooses and enforces with chargebacks.

Each document has one internal source: the order record from the buyer's validated message, the despatch advice and its pallet labels from the warehouse's pack confirmation, the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment and price; a compliance chargeback is a document generated in the wrong place.
An EDI order, like the order that follows a punchout, is a channel into the one order record, keyed on the buyer's order number and GLN and flagged by channel, never a separate order system.

E-invoicing mandates require structured invoices from dated, country-specific deadlines, domestic in scope until ViDA, so the invoice becomes a transmitted document whose status, rejections and archive the issuing ERP holds.

Whatever the route to its partners (portal, integrated provider, in-house EDI, e-document gateway), the company holds the knowledge of each mapping in a partner card with an internal owner, because guidelines change on the partner's schedule.

role.contribution: Gives the part its documents: one internal source per document (the order record, the warehouse's pack confirmation, the ERP's confirmed shipment), the partner card that keeps mapping knowledge inside the company, and the mandate calendar that turns the invoice into a transmitted document with a delivery status.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to order-record: Bergzicht's deduction and Noor's question, then the vocabulary needed to state the answer, then the answer

flow.rationale: Bergzicht's deduction comes first so every term arrives as part of the answer to Noor's question. EDI's vocabulary (what-edi), the documents, the identifiers inside them, the transports and the per-partner guideline follow in that order because each uses the one before: the ASN cannot be explained without the documents, the SSCC rule without the ASN, Peppol's network without transports, chargebacks without guidelines. The rule of one source per document (order-record) comes once all its terms are known, and punchout follows as a second way a buyer's system reaches the same record. The e-invoice follows because it is the third document under a new regime, and the calendar after it because dates mean nothing before the reader knows what is required. The choices and stages come after the requirements they meet, the worked orders after the choices so the reader sees W6's conditions applied, and the failures last, each read against the rule that prevents it. Moving order-record before the vocabulary would state a rule about documents the reader cannot yet name; moving the calendar before the e-invoice section would date an obligation not yet explained.

hook.content: A retail chain sends a purchase order from its own purchasing system and expects a shipment notice describing each pallet and an invoice its accounting software can read; a mismatched pallet label or an unreadable invoice can hold up receiving or payment and trigger a supplier penalty, even when the goods were right.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has sold through a web shop knows the order as something the shop itself creates at checkout.
bridge.to_topic: When the buyer is a large company, the order, the shipment notice and the invoice are documents that travel between two companies' systems, and since 2026 the law sets the form of the invoice, so the question becomes which documents, from which system, by which date.

thesis_statement.text: Trading partners exchange orders, despatch advices and invoices as standard EDI messages, mapped per partner and relayed by a provider or a direct link; each document has one internal source (the order enters the order record like a web order, the despatch advice comes from the warehouse's pack confirmation, the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment), and e-invoicing mandates require structured invoices from dated, country-specific deadlines, so the ERP that issues them holds each invoice's transmission status.

evidence.shows: The chapter's problem in one case: shipping the goods is only part of fulfilling the order.

evidence.shows: The invoice's form is now set by law with dates.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: A Deduction Instead of a Payment
sections.controlling_idea: Bergzicht Outdoor deducted €14,200 from a payment because Kestrel & Pine's ERP wrote the despatch advices before packing while the WMS labeled the pallets it actually built, and W6 answers Noor Visser's question of which system knows the truth each document carries.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the chapter answers: a compliance chargeback caused by a document generated in the wrong system and mappings known only to an outside consultant.

flow.rationale: The partner and its documents first, then the short payment, its name, its cause and the decision that fixed it, in the order Kestrel & Pine met them; the cause only makes sense once the reader knows what the deduction was for.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's claim and roadmap, which start from Bergzicht's deduction.
transition_in.introduces: The deduction itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Bergzicht Outdoor, a Dutch chain worth €2.1 million a year to Kestrel & Pine, has ordered since 2025 through an EDI provider (a value-added network) using three main messages: ORDERS, DESADV and INVOIC.

evidence.what: Bergzicht: 38 shops, Zwolle DC, €2.1M a year, EDI since 2025; the EDI provider; ORDERS, DESADV, INVOIC.
evidence.shows: Introduces the partner, the intermediary and the three documents of the case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In October 2026 Head of Wholesale Lea Moreau received a payment €14,200 short, because Bergzicht charged for nine third-quarter deliveries whose pallet labels did not match the despatch advice.

evidence.what: €14,200 deducted from an October 2026 payment for nine Q3 2026 deliveries; compliance fee plus manual counting.
evidence.shows: The chargeback the chapter explains.

transition_in.introduces: What went wrong with it: a short payment.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: This is the ASN Chargeback: ASN, the advance shipping notice, is another name for the despatch advice, and the deduction is a supplier-compliance penalty, not a card-payment dispute.

transition_in.introduces: Its name in the book and what kind of deduction it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Lea and the lead integration engineer, Ruben Alves, needed two weeks to reconstruct the cause because only an external consultant knew the mappings: the ERP wrote the despatch advice at release, before packing, with ERP pallet numbers, while the WMS printed its own labels at pack time, so merged or split pallets made labels and messages disagree.

evidence.what: Before W6: DESADV from the ERP at release with pallet numbers from an ERP range; WMS labels at pack time; merged or split pallets.
evidence.shows: Shows the document came from a system that did not know the pallets.

evidence.what: Figure 1: the ERP's despatch advice before packing against the WMS's from the pack confirmation.
evidence.shows: Shows the two flows side by side, the rejected scan and the matching one.

transition_in.introduces: Its mechanism and why it was hard to find.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Noor Visser's question, which system knows the truth each document claims to carry, is the chapter's question, and W6 answered it here: pallet labels from the WMS at pack time, the despatch advice from the WMS pack confirmation, and one EDI partner card per trading partner, a record the company keeps of the partner's identifiers, message versions, mapping and internal owner.

evidence.what: W6: SSCC labels generated by the WMS at pack time; DESADV sent from the WMS confirmation; one EDI partner card per trading partner.
evidence.shows: The decision that applies the chapter's rule.

transition_in.carries_over: The mechanism: a document written by a system that did not know the pallets.
transition_in.introduces: The question it raises and Waypoint's answer, W6.

sections.heading: What EDI Is and Why It Has Not Gone Away
sections.controlling_idea: EDI is agreed message formats plus a way of delivering them, with two dominant standards, and it persists because buyers choose it, its documents carry meaning, networks make change costly and regulators accommodate it.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the vocabulary (message, standard, transport, mapping) and the reasons the buyer, not the merchant, decides the format.

flow.rationale: The four words first, then the standards, the evidence of what is used, and only then why it persists, which needs all of them.

transition_in.carries_over: Bergzicht's three EDI messages and W6.
transition_in.introduces: What EDI is in general and why it persists.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In plain words, EDI is a set of agreed message formats plus a way of delivering them: a message is a document such as an order, a standard says which fields it has, a transport is how the file travels and a mapping translates between the standard's fields and your own system's.

Two standards dominate: UN/EDIFACT, with the GS1 EANCOM subset that European retail uses, and ANSI X12 in North America; a brand selling to a Dutch and a US chain needs both, and the message pairs are functional equivalents, not field-for-field translations.

evidence.what: UN/EDIFACT, ISO 9735 (1987); GS1 EANCOM manual (2002 edition, updated 2021); ANSI X12.
evidence.shows: Names the standards and their scope.

transition_in.introduces: The two standards that dominate.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: GS1's 2021 survey, the most recent public one, found ORDERS, INVOIC and DESADV the most implemented EANCOM messages and AS2 the most used transport, and the standards have barely changed since.

evidence.what: GS1 EDI implementation survey 2021: ORDERS, INVOIC, DESADV most implemented; AS2 most used.
evidence.shows: The three documents of the chapter are the core of EDI in practice.

transition_in.introduces: Which of their messages and transports are used most.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A 1980s format still carries wholesale orders first because the buyer chooses: Jumbo's 2026 purchasing conditions oblige suppliers to send order, despatch advice and invoice by EDI, charge €70 per message otherwise and allow deliveries without DESADV and SSCC to be refused.

evidence.what: Jumbo purchasing conditions of 9 April 2026: 'undertake to conduct all communication concerning the flow of goods ... via EDI'; €70 per message; refusal without DESADV and SSCC.
evidence.shows: A buyer imposes the format and enforces it with money.

transition_in.introduces: The first of four reasons it persists: the buyer chooses.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three further reasons keep EDI in place: its documents carry stable meaning, a chain that has mapped hundreds of suppliers would pay more to change than to keep it, and regulators accommodate it, as Germany does by tolerating EDI procedures that do not yet meet its e-invoice rules (explained later in the chapter) to the end of 2027.

evidence.what: Germany tolerates EDI procedures that do not yet meet the e-invoice requirements until the end of 2027.
evidence.shows: Even the regulator accommodates EDI.

transition_in.carries_over: The first reason, the buyer's choice.
transition_in.introduces: The other three reasons.

sections.heading: The Documents: Order, Despatch Advice, Invoice
sections.controlling_idea: Five documents make up the exchange, each with a sender and an internal system of truth; the ASN is the receiving plan keyed by the pallet label, and a syntax acknowledgment says only that a file could be parsed.

advances_thesis.how: Names the documents and the system of truth for each, and the two misreadings (the ASN as paperwork, the acknowledgment as acceptance) that cost money.

transition_in.introduces: Each document, its sender and its internal system of truth.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five documents make up the exchange, three that carry the business (order, despatch advice, invoice) and two that answer them (order response, syntax acknowledgment), each with an EDIFACT and an X12 name, a sender and an internal system of truth.

evidence.what: The five documents: ORDERS/850, ORDRSP/855, DESADV/856, INVOIC/810, CONTRL/997, with sender, content and internal system of truth.
evidence.shows: Each document has its own sender and its own source of truth.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ASN is a message sent at despatch that tells the receiver what is coming pallet by pallet, so receipt can be scanned instead of counted, and Jumbo refuses a delivery without it: the ASN is the receiving plan and the pallet label the key into it.

evidence.what: Jumbo mechanized-DC guidelines (2025-10): every delivery 'must be preceded by a DESADV message'; 'a delivery without an accompanying DESADV message cannot be processed and is therefore refused'; 'the SSCC label forms the link with the DESADV'.
evidence.shows: The ASN decides whether a delivery is received.

transition_in.introduces: The one that decides whether a delivery is received: the ASN.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A CONTRL or 997 says only that a file could be parsed, not that the order was accepted, the delivery received or the invoice will be paid, and treating it as acceptance is a common and expensive mistake.

transition_in.carries_over: The ASN, a document receivers act on.
transition_in.introduces: The acknowledgment, a document readers over-read.

sections.heading: Identifiers: What, Where and This Pallet
sections.controlling_idea: EDI works because both sides use GS1's numbers for products (GTIN), parties and places (GLN) and pallets (SSCC), and the ASN ties them together, so the SSCC must come from the system that builds the pallet.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the identifiers the ASN is built from and derives the rule that the pallet's number comes from the system that packs it.

transition_in.carries_over: The ASN as a receiving plan keyed by the pallet label.
transition_in.introduces: The numbers in that label and in the documents.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: GS1's General Specifications define a GTIN for what is sold, a GLN for who and where, and an SSCC for this pallet, and retailers such as Jumbo and bol require them in the messages.

evidence.what: GS1 General Specifications Release 26.0: the SSCC 'is the only GS1 key that SHALL be used as the identifier of a logistic unit'; bol SSCC labels mandatory since 31 December 2021; Jumbo's GLN rule.
evidence.shows: The identifiers are standard and enforced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ASN ties the three together, listing for each SSCC the GTINs and quantities it holds from one GLN to another, hence the rule Kestrel & Pine paid for: the SSCC must be generated by the system that physically builds the pallet.

evidence.what: An ERP that invents pallet numbers before packing is wrong whenever the warehouse deviates from the plan.
evidence.shows: Derives the chapter's first ownership rule from the identifiers.

transition_in.introduces: How the ASN combines them and the rule that follows.

sections.heading: Transport: Point-to-Point or Network
sections.controlling_idea: Documents travel point-to-point (AS2, SFTP), where every partner is a relationship to manage, or over a network (a VAN, Peppol), where one connection reaches many; Peppol alone has a public directory and mandates the document format.

advances_thesis.how: Explains how documents travel and introduces Peppol's four-corner model that the e-invoice uses.

transition_in.carries_over: The documents and the numbers in them.
transition_in.introduces: How the documents travel.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: AS2 and SFTP are point-to-point, while a VAN and Peppol are networks you connect to once; Peppol alone has a public directory and mandates the document format, and in its four-corner model the sender's access point delivers to the receiver's without a bilateral agreement.

evidence.what: AS2 (RFC 4130), SFTP, VAN, Peppol: what each is, what you connect to, typical use.
evidence.shows: Contrasts point-to-point and network transports.

sections.heading: Mapping, Onboarding and the Chargeback Economy
sections.controlling_idea: The standards are public but every chain publishes its own guideline, so mapping is done and maintained per partner, which is the EDI providers' business, and chargebacks enforce the guideline; data and label chargebacks are an architecture problem.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the cost and the risk of EDI are per partner, and that one family of chargebacks comes from which system produces a document.

transition_in.introduces: The per-partner guideline and its enforcement.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every chain publishes its own message implementation guideline, so mapping is done and maintained per partner, which is the business EDI providers sell, and a retailer like Jumbo offers a cheap portal to small suppliers and an integrated route that needs IT effort.

evidence.what: SPS Commerce 10-K for 2025: 'connect once and immediately transact with thousands of trading partners'; $751.5 million revenue, 96% recurring.
evidence.shows: Per-partner mapping is a large business.

evidence.what: Jumbo: WebEDI 'the simplest, and cheapest in the short term'; integration 'requires translating EDI messages to and from your internal system'.
evidence.shows: The two routes a buyer offers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chargebacks enforce the guideline in two families, delivery performance and data and label compliance; the first is a logistics problem and the second an architecture problem, because the ASN is only as right as the system that generated it.

evidence.what: Walmart's on-time-in-full 3% fee at launch in 2017 (thresholds since raised; no official page); Jumbo €250 per order under 90% of a line; Jumbo €70 per message.
evidence.shows: Examples of each family.

transition_in.introduces: How the buyer enforces it: chargebacks.

sections.heading: How EDI Documents Reach the Order Record and the Ledger
sections.controlling_idea: An EDI order is a channel into the one order record, not a separate order system, and each document then has its own internal source and its own requirements for freshness, consistency, speed and availability.

advances_thesis.how: States the chapter's rule: one order record for every channel and one honest source per document.

transition_in.carries_over: Data and label chargebacks as an architecture problem.
transition_in.introduces: The architecture that prevents them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Data and label chargebacks are prevented where documents are produced, and every document starts from the order record: an EDI order is a channel into it, not a separate order system, so an ORDERS message creates the same order object as a web order, flagged by channel; Kestrel & Pine in January 2027 kept EDI, web and marketplace orders in three places, and the ERP stays the interim home of EDI orders until the OMS takes them in Q4 2027.

evidence.what: January 2027: EDI orders in the ERP, web orders in the shop platform, marketplace orders in the connector; the OMS takes EDI orders from the ERP in Q4 2027.
evidence.shows: The failure the rule prevents, at Kestrel & Pine.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Building on the Documents table's systems of truth, each document has one internal source and never another: the order record from the validated ORDERS, the order response from the record after allocation, the despatch advice from the WMS pack confirmation, the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment and contract price.

evidence.what: Document / produced from / never from / why, for the order record, order response, despatch advice and invoice.
evidence.shows: Gives each document's one source and the wrong source to avoid.

transition_in.carries_over: The order record as the one home for EDI orders, and the Documents table's systems of truth.
transition_in.introduces: What each document must never be produced from, and why.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The flows differ in how fresh, consistent, fast and available they must be, so one integration flow on one schedule cannot serve them: ORDERS in must be exactly once, DESADV out must match the labels and leave before the truck arrives, invoices must be immutable once numbered and rejections tracked, and transmission status kept as evidence.

evidence.what: How fresh, consistent, fast and available each flow must be (ORDERS in, DESADV out, invoice out, status back).
evidence.shows: The flows differ, so one system cannot serve all of them the same way.

transition_in.introduces: What each flow requires.

sections.heading: Punchout: When the Buyer's System Owns the Order
sections.controlling_idea: In punchout the buyer shops in the supplier's web shop from inside its procurement system, which owns the requisition and the purchase order, so a punchout cart is never an order and the real order enters the same order record later.

advances_thesis.how: Extends the one-order-record rule to buyers who send no ORDERS but shop through their own system.

transition_in.carries_over: The EDI order as a channel into the order record.
transition_in.introduces: A second way a buyer's own system reaches it: punchout.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Some corporate buyers send no ORDERS but shop in the supplier's web shop from inside their procurement system, as the cXML User's Guide and SAP's OCI describe.

evidence.what: cXML User's Guide 1.2.037: procurement applications 'display a button instead of product or pricing details' ... a button 'returns the order information to the procurement application'; OCI posts cart lines to a hook URL.
evidence.shows: Defines punchout from its protocol.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Punchout inverts the usual flow: the buyer's system owns the requisition and the purchase order, the shop is only a catalog session, and the real order arrives later as a cXML order request or an EDI ORDERS, so the shop must never treat a punchout cart as an order.

transition_in.introduces: What it means for the order record.

sections.heading: E-Invoicing: The Invoice Becomes a Transmitted Legal Document
sections.controlling_idea: An e-invoice is a structured document in three layers (EN 16931, UBL, Peppol BIS Billing 3.0) that differs from an EDI INVOIC in almost everything but its claim, and it makes the issuing system hold transmission status, rejections and archive.

advances_thesis.how: Explains what the mandates require and why the invoice becomes a document with a delivery state held by the ERP.

transition_in.carries_over: The documents of supply-chain EDI, whose format the buyer sets.
transition_in.introduces: The invoice, whose format the law now sets.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The European Commission defines an e-invoice as structured data for automatic processing, not a PDF, and it has three layers to keep apart: the EN 16931 semantic model, the UBL syntax and the Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 profile, whose own releases have dates.

evidence.what: European Commission: an electronic invoice is one 'issued, transmitted and received in a structured data format which allows for its automatic and electronic processing'; Peppol BIS 3.0.21 published 20 May 2026, mandatory 17 August 2026.
evidence.shows: Defines the e-invoice and shows even its format has a calendar.

evidence.what: Figure 2: Peppol's four-corner model, with the transmission status flowing back to the issuing system.
evidence.shows: Shows how a Peppol invoice travels and what comes back.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An EDI INVOIC and a Peppol invoice carry the same claim and differ in who defines the content, purpose, addressing, transport, validation and legal weight.

evidence.what: EDI INVOIC against Peppol/EN 16931 invoice on six rows.
evidence.shows: The two invoices are different documents for different purposes.

transition_in.introduces: How it differs from the EDI INVOIC the chapter already met.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three things change for the architecture: the system that issues invoices, usually the ERP, holds transmission status, rejections and archive; in clearance countries the state platform sits in the invoice path; and commerce platforms do not issue the tax invoice, their PDF being a courtesy copy.

evidence.what: Figure 3: a PDF e-mailed into an inbox against a structured invoice sent through a network with its delivered status returned and stored.
evidence.shows: Shows the invoice gaining a delivery state the issuer must hold.

transition_in.introduces: What it changes in the systems.

sections.heading: The Mandate Calendar
sections.controlling_idea: The mandates have official dates per country as of November 2026, they are domestic in scope, and ViDA brings the cross-border case in 2030, so building the capability once is cheaper than per deadline.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the dated obligations and their scope so the reader can place a company on the calendar.

transition_in.carries_over: What an e-invoice is and what it changes.
transition_in.introduces: When and where it is required, starting with Belgium's mandate as announced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Belgium's mandate shows what the e-invoice means in practice: the government announced in September 2024 that from 1 January 2026 PDF invoices by e-mail would no longer be enough, and in December 2025 confirmed a three-month tolerance on penalties and refused a general postponement.

evidence.what: einvoice.belgium.be, 18 September 2024: 'all Belgian enterprises liable to VAT will have to use structured electronic invoices'; 'sending a PDF invoice by e-mail or via a platform will no longer be enough'; 'via a decentralised network called Peppol'; 18 December 2025 tolerance.
evidence.shows: The mandate in the government's own words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The mandate dates as of November 2026, from tax administrations and the Commission, are the chapter's most volatile facts: Belgium since 1 January 2026, Germany receiving since 2025 and issuing from 2027 or 2028, France from September 2026, Italy since 2019, Poland from 2026, the Netherlands planned for 2030 and ViDA from 1 July 2030.

evidence.what: Seven rows (Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Poland, Netherlands, ViDA): what is mandatory, since when, format and channel, whether it touches Kestrel & Pine.
evidence.shows: The calendar the reader places a company on.
evidence.source: einvoice.belgium.be; BMF; impots.gouv.fr; European Commission; gov.pl; Rijksoverheid

transition_in.introduces: The full calendar of mandates, Belgium's among them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two readings follow: the mandates are domestic, so whether a Dutch supplier is bound in Belgium is not settled and is a question for a tax adviser while Belgian customers expect Peppol anyway, and ViDA brings the cross-border case in 2030, so the capability is cheaper built once than per deadline, before the Long Fuse burns down.

evidence.what: Belgium's FAQ: VAT-registered persons not established in Belgium and without a permanent establishment are not subject (law still being amended); Germany covers domestic transactions.
evidence.shows: The scope is domestic and, for a foreign supplier, hedged.

transition_in.introduces: How a newcomer should read it.

flow.rationale: Belgium's mandate in the government's words first, because it is the one Kestrel & Pine meets; then the whole calendar with Belgium as one row, then how to read its scope, which needs both.

sections.heading: The Choices
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant connects through a provider's portal, an integrated provider, in-house EDI or an e-document gateway, chosen by partners and countries, and whichever it picks the ASN must come from the WMS and the company must hold a partner card per partner.

advances_thesis.how: Lets the reader choose a route and states the two conditions that hold on every route.

flow.rationale: From the smallest commitment to the largest, so each route is read against the one before; the recommendation comes after the comparison table it rests on.

transition_in.carries_over: The documents, their sources and the dated obligations.
transition_in.introduces: The ways a merchant can meet them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A provider's web portal needs no integration and suits small suppliers, but it is retyping and does not scale past a few orders a day.

A provider integrated with your systems maps the chain's guideline to your order record, WMS and ERP, often through an iPaaS; the provider owns the mappings, you own what each document means, and this is the common choice at Kestrel & Pine's size.

transition_in.introduces: Integration through the provider.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In-house EDI gives full control at full cost and makes sense only when EDI is the business.

transition_in.introduces: The merchant owning everything.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An e-document gateway produces and receives every structured document from the same internal records with per-partner and per-country rules as configuration, and the integrated provider grows into it as partners and countries multiply.

evidence.what: Portal, integrated provider, in-house, gateway on time to first partner, running cost, mapping ownership, chargeback exposure and when each is right.
evidence.shows: Compares the four routes on the reader's decision criteria.

transition_in.introduces: One component for every structured document.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author recommends the integrated provider at the Omnichannel stage on two non-optional conditions, the ASN from the WMS pack confirmation and a partner card per trading partner in the company's own repository, because the provider may hold the mapping but the company must hold the knowledge.

transition_in.introduces: The author's choice and its conditions.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: Each scale stage has its typical EDI and e-invoicing setup, what becomes necessary and the signs of outgrowing it, and Kestrel & Pine runs a stage 2 setup at stage 3, which the deduction signalled.

advances_thesis.how: Says which route fits which stage and places Kestrel & Pine.

transition_in.carries_over: The four routes and the recommendation.
transition_in.introduces: Which fits at which stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the time of the deduction Kestrel & Pine sat at stage 3 with a stage 2 setup, one chain, one provider, mappings built by one consultant and the ASN from the wrong system, and the deduction was the warning sign.

evidence.what: Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group: what is typical, what becomes necessary, warning signs.
evidence.shows: Gives the stage-specific setup and signals.

sections.heading: In Practice
sections.controlling_idea: Bergzicht's spring reorder under W6 and a Belgian Peppol invoice show the rules at work: each document from its source and the invoice sent with its status kept.

advances_thesis.how: Runs the chapter's rules through one EDI order and one Peppol invoice with ledger figures.

flow.rationale: The EDI order from receipt to invoice, then the Belgian order from order to invoice and the reason for sending it over Peppol.

transition_in.carries_over: The stage table and Kestrel & Pine's place on it.
transition_in.introduces: The rules applied to two orders after W6.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On 6 April 2027 the EDI provider delivers Bergzicht's ORDERS for 240 units across 18 SKUs, €19,860 excluding VAT, and the ERP resolves the item codes, checks contract prices and creates the order, because the OMS is not live until Q4.

evidence.what: ORDERS 6 April 2027, 240 units, 18 SKUs, €19,860 excl. VAT; ERP creates the order; OMS from Q4 2027.
evidence.shows: The order enters one record from the buyer's message.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The warehouse reserves the units, an ORDRSP confirms the lines, the WMS prints one SSCC label for each of three pallets at packing, and the DESADV comes from that same pack confirmation and reaches Zwolle before delivery on 9 April.

evidence.what: Three pallets with SSCC labels; DESADV from the pack confirmation; delivered to Zwolle 9 April.
evidence.shows: The despatch advice comes from the system that built the pallets.

transition_in.introduces: Allocation, packing and the despatch advice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ERP issues the INVOIC on 9 April for the shipped quantities at contract prices, due 9 May, and this is W6 in practice: labels and shipment notice describe the same packed pallets, which in Q3 2026 they did not.

evidence.what: INVOIC 9 April, payment due 9 May; contrast with Q3 2026.
evidence.shows: The invoice comes from the confirmed shipment, and the case closes against the scene.

evidence.what: Figure 4: Bergzicht's spring reorder as a document cycle, three documents from three systems of truth.
evidence.shows: Shows the whole exchange and where each document comes from.

transition_in.introduces: The invoice and what W6 changed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ardennes Trail Co., a fictional shop in Namur and one of the 210 Belgian accounts, orders 40 Ridgewalker jackets at €95, €3,800 excluding VAT, through the B2B portal on Wednesday 21 April 2027.

evidence.what: Ardennes Trail Co., Namur; 40 jackets at €95 = €3,800; B2B portal; 21 April 2027.
evidence.shows: The Belgian variant.

transition_in.carries_over: An EDI order to a Dutch chain.
transition_in.introduces: A portal order from a Belgian shop that needs a Peppol invoice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At dispatch on 23 April the ERP issues the invoice in its numbering sequence, an intra-EU supply at 0% VAT with the reverse-charge mention, due 23 May, as a UBL document under Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 sent through the EDI provider as access point, and stores the transmission status.

evidence.what: Invoice 23 April by bpost dispatch; 0% reverse charge; due 23 May; Peppol BIS 3.0 via the EDI provider's access point; status stored in the ERP.
evidence.shows: The invoice is issued by the ERP and kept with its delivery state.

transition_in.introduces: Its invoice over Peppol.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine has sent Peppol invoices to all Belgian business customers since January 2026 by choice, not because the mandate is known to bind a Dutch supplier, because larger customers' bookkeeping expects Peppol and one rule was cheaper than exceptions.

evidence.what: Peppol to all Belgian business customers since January 2026, by choice.
evidence.shows: Hedged per consistency ruling 5.

transition_in.carries_over: The Peppol invoice to Ardennes Trail Co.
transition_in.introduces: Why Kestrel & Pine sends one at all.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Five failures (a duplicate ORDERS, a changed guideline, the ASN from the wrong system, a rejected e-invoice, a provider outage or a departing consultant) each have a detection and a recovery that follow from the chapter's rules.

advances_thesis.how: Reads each failure against the rule that prevents it.

flow.rationale: The failures in the order of the document cycle: order in, partner rules, despatch advice, invoice, then the intermediary and the people around all of them.

transition_in.carries_over: The rules working in the two orders.
transition_in.introduces: What happens when they are broken.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A duplicate ORDERS after a timeout that was a success creates two orders unless handling is idempotent: the buyer's order number plus GLN is the natural key, so a second ORDERS with it is a duplicate or a change, never a new order.

A changed guideline sent to the consultant's address shows up as a refused truck, the Pulled Rug; the partner card's internal owner and the scorecard detect it, and a versioned, tested mapping recovers.

transition_in.carries_over: A failure in the order flow.
transition_in.introduces: A failure in the partner's rules.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ASN from the wrong system, Kestrel & Pine's case, is detected by comparing every DESADV with the WMS pack confirmation before sending and recovered by a corrected DESADV or a dispute backed by the pack record and label log.

transition_in.introduces: The chapter's own case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A rejected e-invoice, numbered in the ERP but never received, is detected by a transmission-status field and a daily 'issued but not delivered' report, and recovered by a re-send or a credit note and new invoice as the country's rules require.

transition_in.introduces: The invoice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A provider outage loses nothing if every document is persisted before sending with a reference the provider can deduplicate and a heartbeat per partner, and a departing consultant costs little if the partner card and a mapping export sit in the company's own repository.

transition_in.introduces: Failures of the intermediary and of the knowledge.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The chain's purchase order, despatch advice and invoice of the opening are three documents with three sources: Bergzicht's €14,200 deduction came from a despatch advice written by the ERP before anyone packed, and the e-invoice adds a delivery state to the third document; every compliance chargeback in the public rule sets is a document generated in the wrong place.
conclusion.so_what: The remedies are ownership rules, not a new provider: the despatch advice and labels from the WMS, the invoice from the ERP with its transmission status, EDI orders in the one order record, a partner card per trading partner and a dated mandate calendar with an owner.

callback.to: The introduction's retail chain whose pallet labels or invoice can hold up receiving or payment and trigger a penalty.
callback.how: Paragraph p52 answers it with Bergzicht's deduction and the three sources.

takeaway.content: For each trading partner, name the system that generates each document, compare every despatch advice with the pack confirmation, keep a partner card, and place your company on the mandate calendar.

hand_off.carries_over: The documents of the EDI chapter, which end in the ledger: invoices and credit notes the ERP numbers and issues, with their transmission status, and the terms, credit limits and wholesale prices the B2B chapter assigned to the ERP.
hand_off.introduces: What the ERP, the system that keeps the ledger, should own in a commerce business, what it receives and how often, and whether it should be the hub everything else connects through.

transition_in.carries_over: The failures and how each is detected.
transition_in.introduces: The chapter's answer set against its opening, then what holds, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opening's retail chain asked for a purchase order, a per-pallet shipment notice and a readable invoice, and the chapter's answer is that the three documents the chain asked for have three different sources: Bergzicht's €14,200 came from a despatch advice the ERP wrote before packing, so the penalty is explained by the system that wrote the document, not by the pickers, and the e-invoice adds a delivery state to the third.

evidence.what: The opening's three documents set against the ASN Chargeback and the e-invoice.
evidence.shows: The reader can now explain the penalty by the system that wrote the document.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: EDI's standards, identifiers and transports and its three most implemented documents; the ASN as a receiving plan keyed by the SSCC label that receivers refuse deliveries without; and the dated e-invoicing obligations.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's answer in one paragraph.
transition_in.introduces: The points it rests on, starting with what the sources establish.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Depends on context: which route fits (portal, integrated provider, in-house, gateway), whether a foreign supplier is bound by a domestic mandate, and whether EDI orders live in the OMS or, before one exists, in the ERP.

transition_in.introduces: What depends on the merchant's situation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: each document has exactly one honest source that the architecture should enforce, and the e-invoice gives the ERP the same discipline as the order channel (persistence before sending, idempotent re-sends, a status per document, a daily report of what was issued but not received).

transition_in.carries_over: What is established and what depends on context.
transition_in.introduces: The author's own judgement, labelled as such.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eight questions let the reader find, in their own company, the partners' EDI conditions, which system generates the DESADV, where EDI orders live, the partner cards, the ASN match rate and its owner, the mandates per country, the invoice issuer's status and archive, and who can read the mappings.

transition_in.introduces: Questions that apply them to the reader's own company.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The documents end in the ledger, so the next chapter asks what the ERP, the system that keeps it, should own in a commerce business and whether it should be the hub everything connects through.
